q: A cool bag contains ice and water at 0 °C, and heat comes through the walls all the time. Why does the inside temperature of the bag not rise until all the ice has melted?
a: The energy coming through the wall is used to melt the ice, $Q = sm$, and not to raise the temperature. During a change of state the temperature stays at the melting point, and only when the ice has melted does the energy start to raise the temperature of the water.

q: How much energy is needed to melt 0.40 kg of ice at 0 °C and warm the water that forms to 25 °C? Use the values $s = 334\,\text{kJ/kg}$ and $c = 4190\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}}$.
a: Melting: $Q_1 = sm = 334\,\text{kJ/kg} \cdot 0.40\,\text{kg} = 133.6\,\text{kJ}$. Warming: $Q_2 = cm\Delta T = 4190\,\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}} \cdot 0.40\,\text{kg} \cdot 25\,\text{K} = 41.9\,\text{kJ}$. In total $Q = Q_1 + Q_2 = 175.5\,\text{kJ} \approx 1.8 \cdot 10^2\,\text{kJ}$, two significant figures like the mass $0.40\,\text{kg}$.

q: Sauna water is thrown on hot stones. Why do the stones cool down much more when the water vaporises than if it only warmed to 100 °C?
a: The water also vaporises, and vaporisation needs energy $Q = rm$, which is about 2260 kJ/kg. This is many times more than heating the water: 1 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C needs only 335 kJ. The energy is taken from the stones, so they cool down.
